# Introduction

This application estimates the **total number of species expected to exist** in a
taxonomic group ($S_T$) from a time series of species descriptions, using a
Bayesian hierarchical model. It generalizes the framework applied to Brazilian
Dactylogyridae (parasitic flatworms) and their freshwater Actinopterygii (bony
fish) hosts in Boeger et al. (submitted, *Zoologia*, manuscript
ZOOL-2026-0012.R1), which in turn adapts the species-discovery models of Pimm
et al. (2010) and Joppa et al. (2011).

**The app is not restricted to any particular taxon.** You supply your own
species-description records (any parasitic or free-living group), and the app
fits the model to *your* data with *your* priors.

Two independent modeling choices combine into up to **four candidate Poisson
model structures**, plus an optional third choice — swapping the Poisson
likelihood for a Negative Binomial one — adds two more (for **six candidate
structures** in total; §2.3). The app fits and statistically compares as
many of them as you select, letting your data, not a guess, indicate which
formula describes it best (§2.5):

- **Host term**: on (parasitic mode, with a defined host pool) or off
  (free-living mode, or parasitic data without a usable host pool).
- **Efficiency-trend form**: exponential or linear change in taxonomic
  efficiency over time (§2.3).

No dataset, credential, or analysis result is stored by the application beyond
your browser session. See §6 ("Data Handling & Privacy") for details.

# Scientific Background & Method

## The discovery process

The number of *new* species described in time interval $i$, $S_i$, is modeled
as a random draw from a Poisson process:

$$S_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$$

where the rate $\lambda_i$ depends on (a) how many species remain to be
discovered, (b) how much taxonomic effort was applied, (c) for parasitic
taxa, how many host species remain available to be surveyed, and (d) a trend
in baseline taxonomic efficiency over time. Following Pimm et al. (2010),
Joppa et al. (2011), and Boeger et al. (submitted), this is stated as a
**product** of those four factors — e.g. for the host + exponential-trend
structure:

$$
\lambda_i \;=\; \underbrace{T_i}_{\text{effort}}
\;\cdot\; \underbrace{(S_T - \text{cumS}_i)}_{\text{species remaining}}
\;\cdot\; \underbrace{(H_t - \text{cumH}_i)}_{\text{hosts remaining}}
\;\cdot\; \underbrace{L_0\, e^{\beta Y_i}}_{\text{efficiency at time } Y_i}
$$

equivalent to the published form
$S_i/[T_i(S_T-\text{cumS}_i)(H_t-\text{cumH}_i)] = \exp(\log L_0 + \beta Y_i)$
with $L_0 \equiv a$. **The app fits this exact rate**, but internally in
*log* form, because Stan's numerically stable Poisson likelihood
(`poisson_log`) takes $\log \lambda_i$ directly rather than $\lambda_i$
itself (avoiding overflow/underflow, since $\lambda_i$ spans many orders of
magnitude across intervals). Taking $\log$ of the product above is a single,
exact algebraic step — $\log(xyz) = \log x + \log y + \log z$ turns the
product into a sum, nothing more:

$$
\log \lambda_i \;=\; \underbrace{\log T_i}_{\text{effort}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log(S_T - \text{cumS}_i)}_{\text{species remaining}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log(H_t - \text{cumH}_i)}_{\text{hosts remaining (host structures only)}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log L_i}_{\text{efficiency at time } Y_i}
$$

This is the form actually evaluated by the fitted Stan code; it is
numerically a different *representation* of the same $\lambda_i$, not a
different model. $L_i$, the efficiency term, takes one of two forms
depending on your chosen **trend form** — see §2.3 for both exact equations
(both in product form and in the equivalent log form the app fits).
*Implementation note:* to keep $\log T_i$ finite for any interval with zero
active taxonomists, the fitted model evaluates $\log(1+T_i)$ rather than
$\log T_i$ — a standard Laplace-style safeguard that is numerically
indistinguishable from $\log T_i$ whenever $T_i \geq$ a few, and only changes
behavior for empty (zero-effort) intervals, where it keeps their
contribution finite instead of $-\infty$.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $S_T$ | **Total number of species expected to exist** in the group — the key quantity of interest. |
| $L_0$ | Baseline taxonomic discovery efficiency at the reference year (parameterization depends on trend form — §2.3). |
| $\beta$ | Trend in discovery efficiency over time. Positive = taxonomists are getting relatively more efficient at finding remaining species over time; negative = the opposite (e.g., the "easy" species were found first). |
| $Y_i$ | Centered end-year of interval $i$ (years minus the mean year, so $L_0$ refers to the middle of your time series, not year zero). |
| $\text{cumS}_i$ | Cumulative species described **before** interval $i$ began. |
| $T_i$ | Number of unique taxonomists (authors) active in interval $i$ — a proxy for research effort. |
| $H_t$ | Total known/expected host-species pool (host structures only) — a fixed number you supply, not fitted. |
| $\text{cumH}_i$ | Cumulative unique host species recorded **before** interval $i$ (host structures only; computed automatically from your `animalHostNames` column). |

Intuitively: as more species are described ($\text{cumS}_i$ grows toward
$S_T$), the pool of undescribed species shrinks, and the expected discovery
rate declines — unless rising effort ($T_i$) or efficiency ($L_0, \beta$)
compensates. Fitting this model to your observed $(S_i, T_i)$ time series lets
the Bayesian posterior on $S_T$ tell you, with uncertainty, how many species
are likely to exist in total — including the ones not yet described.

## Why Bayesian, and why priors matter

$S_T$ is not identified by the data alone in any strict sense — the model
extrapolates a decelerating discovery curve toward an asymptote it has not
yet observed. The **prior on $S_T$** (a Gamma distribution, parameterized by
shape `alpha` and rate `beta`, with prior mean $= \alpha/\beta$) is therefore
not a formality: it encodes your independent, external belief about the
plausible order of magnitude of total diversity (e.g., from comparable taxa,
expert judgement, or published estimates for sister groups). **The app does
not supply a default $S_T$ prior — you must set one explicitly**, because a
sensible default does not exist across arbitrary taxa. See §4.2 for practical
guidance on choosing `alpha`/`beta`.

The efficiency-intercept and $\beta$ priors are weaker (defaults provided —
§4.2/§2.3) and rarely need adjustment unless you have strong prior knowledge
about the trend in discovery efficiency.

## Structural variants: host term and efficiency-trend form

**Host term** (on/off): the *host* structures add the
$\log(H_t - \text{cumH}_i)$ term, reflecting the hypothesis that parasite
discovery is partly contingent on finding new host species to examine. You
supply $H_t$ (a single fixed number: your best estimate of the total
host-species pool) and the app computes $\text{cumH}_i$ automatically from the
`animalHostNames` column. The *no-host* structures omit that term; they are
the only option in free-living mode.

> **$H_t$'s dual role, and why you should sensitivity-test it.** $H_t$ often
> ends up informing your analysis twice: once as the fixed ceiling in the
> host term above, and again if you derive your $S_T$ prior mean from it
> (e.g. "$S_T \approx k \times H_t$" for some assumed parasite/host ratio
> $k$ — exactly how the source manuscript's P1–P6 scenarios were built).
> That's not invalid — external information may legitimately inform a prior
> — but it does mean an error in your $H_t$ estimate propagates through
> *both* channels at once rather than being caught by one independent line
> of evidence checking the other. The manuscript's own result illustrates
> the effect starkly: $S_T$ ranged from 7,491 (documented $H_t=3{,}732$) to
> 50,975 (estimated $H_t=7{,}991$ with a higher ratio) — "highly dependent
> on the assumed total richness of … hosts," in the authors' words. Two
> ways to check how much your own conclusion rests on getting $H_t$ right:
> (1) compare host vs. no-host structures (§2.5) — if a host structure
> doesn't clearly outperform its no-host counterpart on LOO-ELPD/CRPS, the
> host term isn't earning its keep beyond whatever the prior already
> encodes; (2) run the **sensitivity battery** (§4.3) with a *different*
> $H_t$ per scenario — the battery form lets each scenario override $H_t$,
> so one run can cross several $H_t$ assumptions against several $S_T$-prior
> scenarios and show you the resulting spread directly, the same way Table 4
> of the source manuscript does.

**Efficiency-trend form** (exponential/linear): the two published parent
models use two different assumptions about how baseline efficiency $L_i$
evolves over time. Both are shown below in their original product form
(as in your source formula) and the equivalent log form the app actually
fits (§2.1's product-to-sum identity applied to $L_i$ alone):

- **Exponential trend** (used for Dactylogyridae in Boeger et al.):
  $$L_i = L_0 \cdot e^{\beta Y_i} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log L_i = \log L_0 + \beta Y_i.$$
  Efficiency changes by a constant *proportion* per unit time and can never
  turn negative, whatever $\beta$ is.
- **Linear trend** (the original Pimm et al. 2010 / Joppa et al. 2011 form,
  used for Actinopterygii in Boeger et al.):
  $$L_i = L_0 + \beta Y_i \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log L_i = \log(L_0 + \beta Y_i).$$
  Efficiency changes by a constant *absolute amount* per unit time; note the
  log here is applied to the whole sum $(L_0+\beta Y_i)$, not distributed
  across it — there is no further product to expand. The app floors $L_i$ at
  a small positive value so the Poisson rate (and this log) stays valid even
  where the trend would otherwise cross zero within your observed range.

Crossing these two axes gives **four Poisson structures**: *host +
exponential*, *host + linear*, *no-host + exponential*, *no-host + linear*
(the last two are the only options in free-living mode). Fit two or more of
them together and the app ranks them for you (§2.5) — this is how "which
formula fits my data" gets answered empirically rather than guessed. An
optional Negative-Binomial likelihood adds two more no-host structures —
see below.

> **Practical note on numerical stability.** The *host + linear* combination
> multiplies two large, independently varying "remaining pool" terms
> ($S_T - \text{cumS}_i$ and $H_t - \text{cumH}_i$) by a small additive
> efficiency term, which can produce a harder-to-sample posterior (elevated
> `Rhat`, divergent transitions) than the other three combinations,
> especially with short or noisy time series. If you see poor convergence
> for this specific combination, try: tighter/better-centered priors for
> $L_0$ (order-of-magnitude guidance: roughly
> $\text{mean}(S_i) / [\text{mean}(T_i) \cdot \text{mean}(S_T-\text{cumS}_i) \cdot \text{mean}(H_t-\text{cumH}_i)]$),
> "Full precision" iterations, or compare against the *host + exponential*
> structure instead (which does not share this issue and is what the source
> manuscript uses for its host-covariate model).

## Optional likelihood family: Negative Binomial (overdispersed counts)

All four structures above assume $S_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$,
which constrains the variance of $S_i$ to equal its mean. Real discovery
time series are often **overdispersed** — description activity comes in
bursts (a monograph, a new survey program) rather than at a smooth,
Poisson-regular rate. Boeger et al.'s own Actinopterygii model uses a
**Negative Binomial** likelihood for exactly this reason (their Table 3
reports a fitted dispersion parameter $\phi$, median 3.68, 95% CI
2.31–5.75, and states explicitly that species description "is not uniform
over time … characterized by periods of higher and lower activity than
would be expected under a simple Poisson process").

Two extra structures let you test this on your own data: **no-host +
exponential (Neg. Binomial)** and **no-host + linear (Neg. Binomial)** —
the same mean structure $\lambda_i$ as their Poisson counterparts above,
but $S_i \sim \text{NegBinomial2}(\lambda_i, \phi)$ instead, where $\phi$ is
a dispersion parameter ($\phi \to \infty$ recovers the Poisson case;
smaller $\phi$ means more overdispersion). These structures are **no-host
only** (available in both parasitic and free-living mode) — the
host-covariate structures always use Poisson, matching the source
manuscript's own Dactylogyridae model. $\phi$ is not a prior you set: it is
fit with a fixed, weakly-informative log-normal prior
($\log\phi \sim \text{Normal}(\log 5, 1)$, centered near the order of
magnitude the source manuscript found for Actinopterygii) and reported in
the parameter table alongside $S_T$, the efficiency intercept, and $\beta$.

Fit a Negative-Binomial structure alongside its Poisson counterpart and let
LOO-ELPD/CRPS (§2.5) tell you whether the extra dispersion parameter earns
its keep for your data — exactly how the app lets you compare
host-vs-no-host or exponential-vs-linear.

**$S_T$ prior mode for Negative-Binomial structures.** These two structures
offer a second $S_T$-prior option beyond the Gamma prior every other
structure uses: a **bounded (flat)** prior — $S_T$ constrained only to
$[\text{lower}, \text{upper}]$ with no further shape, exactly the approach
the source manuscript used for Actinopterygii (lower = observed total + 10,
upper = observed total $\times$ 10 by default, both overridable). Toggle
this on Tab 2 ("Use a bounded (flat) prior instead of Gamma"); it only
affects whichever Negative-Binomial structure(s) you've selected — any
Poisson structure fit in the same run always uses the Gamma prior. This
toggle is available for single runs only; battery scenarios always use the
Gamma prior for every structure, including Negative-Binomial ones.

> **Practical note.** The bounded/flat $S_T$ prior combined with a
> Negative-Binomial likelihood is a genuinely harder inference problem than
> the Gamma-prior Poisson structures: a wide, uninformative $S_T$ range and
> a freely-fit dispersion parameter are both being estimated from the same
> short time series, which can produce elevated `Rhat`, low `n_eff`, and
> divergent transitions — especially with fewer than roughly 15–20 time
> intervals. This mirrors the source manuscript's own experience: its
> Actinopterygii model used this exact bounded-prior/Negative-Binomial
> combination and required close attention to convergence diagnostics. If
> you see poor convergence: increase iterations ("Full precision"), narrow
> the bounds if you have external information to justify it, or compare
> against the Gamma-prior mode for the same structure (§2.5) to see whether
> the two prior choices materially disagree.


## Model fitting

Models are fit with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan, via `rstan`), sampling
$S_T$, the efficiency intercept, and $\beta$ from their joint posterior. You
control the number of iterations, warmup, and chains (§4.3); more iterations
give more stable estimates at the cost of runtime.

**Convergence diagnostics** (`Rhat`, `n_eff`) are reported alongside every
parameter estimate. As a rule of thumb, `Rhat` should be $\le 1.01$ and
`n_eff` should be in the hundreds or more; if not, increase iterations/warmup
or reconsider the priors (see the numerical-stability note in §2.3).

## Comparing models: letting the data decide the formula

Whenever you fit **two or more structures together** — which happens by
default on Tab 2 (the app pre-selects more than one structure), and always in
the sensitivity battery — the app produces a ranked comparison in addition to
each structure's individual diagnostics, using:

- **LOO-ELPD** (Leave-One-Out Expected Log Predictive Density, via the `loo`
  package): a fully Bayesian estimate of each model's out-of-sample
  generalization. Higher (less negative) is better.
- **CRPS** (Continuous Ranked Probability Score) and **MAE** (Mean Absolute
  Error) of the posterior-predictive distribution against your observed
  $S_i$ time series (via `scoringRules`). Lower is better for both.

Alongside the ELPD-difference and CRPS/MAE bar charts, a **rank-concordance
plot** shows every fitted model's LOO-ELPD rank plotted against its CRPS
rank side by side (1 = best), ordered along the x-axis by CRPS rank — this
directly reproduces Figure 10 of the source manuscript. Large gaps between
the two lines for a given model flag genuine disagreement between the
metrics (the manuscript found this mostly among mid/low-ranked models);
close agreement at the top of the ranking, as in the source study, is a
strong signal that the best-supported model isn't an artifact of picking
one scoring rule over the other.

This is the app's answer to "should I use a linear or exponential trend, and
should I include the host term?" — fit the candidates you want to compare
(any subset of the up to six structures) in a single run, and read off the
best-supported one, rather than assuming an answer in advance.

The **sensitivity battery** (§4.3) extends the same comparison across
*multiple prior scenarios* as well, so you can additionally confirm your
conclusions are not an artifact of one prior choice — this is exactly the
analysis performed in the source manuscript across six prior scenarios.

# Data Requirements

Upload an `.xlsx` or `.csv` file. Column names must match **exactly** (case
sensitive). Any other columns in your file are ignored, except for the
optional Category-filter columns described below.

## Always required

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `scientificName` | text | The species' scientific name. Used to count distinct species per year. |
| `namePublishedInYear` | number | The year the species was formally described/published. |
| `scientificNameAuthorship` | text | The describing author(s), e.g. `"Smith, J. & Jones, A."`. Used only to count unique active taxonomists per year (the effort proxy $T_i$). Names are split on commas, semicolons, ampersands, and the standalone words "and"/"e"/"y" (English/Portuguese/Spanish conjunctions). |

## Required in Parasitic mode only

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `animalHostNames` | text | Semicolon-separated list of host species names for that record, e.g. `"Hostus one; Hostus two"`. Used to compute the cumulative unique-host time series ($\text{cumH}_i$). |

## Optional: Category and Habitat filters (CTFB-style exports)

If your file is a full taxonomic export (e.g. from the Catálogo Taxonômico da
Fauna do Brasil, CTFB) with additional Darwin-Core-style columns, you can
upload it **unfiltered** and let the app do the filtering for you:

| Column | Effect |
|---|---|
| Any of `phylum`, `class`, `subClass`, `infraClass`, `superOrder`, `order`, `subOrder`, `infraOrder`, `superFamily`, `family`, `subFamily`, `tribe`, `subTribe`, `genus`, `subGenus` | If present, Tab 1 shows a **Category** dropdown letting you pick one of these rank columns and a value found in your data (e.g. `family = "Dactylogyridae"`); the app restricts to rows matching that value before doing anything else. |
| Any of `habitat`, `environment`, `SALINITY`, `lifeForm` | If present, Tab 1 shows a **Habitat** dropdown letting you pick one of these columns and a value (e.g. `habitat = "agua doce"` to restrict to freshwater taxa, mirroring the `SALINITY == 'freshwater'` restriction used for Actinopterygii in the source manuscript). Values are matched per semicolon-separated token, so a row recorded as `"agua doce;marinho"` (both freshwater and marine) still matches either `"agua doce"` or `"marinho"` — not just an exact whole-cell match. |
| `taxonomicStatus` / `taxonRank` | If either is present, Tab 1 shows a checkbox **"Restrict to accepted, species-rank names"**, checked by default. Matched case-insensitively against either vocabulary: `taxonomicStatus` is `"NOME_ACEITO"` or `"accepted"` (CTFB Portuguese / Darwin Core English) and/or `taxonRank` is `"ESPECIE"` or `"species"`, so a plain GBIF-style Darwin Core export works the same as a CTFB export. Uncheck it to keep every row regardless of status/rank — needed if you are reproducing a prior analysis (e.g. a published table) that did not apply this restriction, since it can materially change $S_i$ per interval. |

The Category and Habitat filters combine (AND) with each other and with the
status/rank checkbox — e.g. family = "Dactylogyridae" AND habitat =
"agua doce" AND accepted/species-rank restricts to freshwater Dactylogyridae
only. None of these filters is required — if your spreadsheet is already a
clean, pre-filtered list of species records (the minimal schema above), none
of these columns need to exist and nothing changes. A status box on Tab 1
reports exactly which filters were applied and how many rows they removed.

## Data preparation tips

- One row per species record (not per specimen or per locality).
- If you are not using the Category filter, pre-filter your source data to
  the taxon and time window you want modeled *before* uploading — the app
  otherwise treats every row in the uploaded file as belonging to the target
  group.
- Rows with a missing/non-numeric year, missing species name, or (in
  parasitic mode) missing host names are dropped automatically, with the
  cleaned row count shown after upload.
- If your data spans a very long time range with few early records, consider
  setting a later **start year** (§4.2) to exclude a sparse, uninformative
  tail that can destabilize the fit.
- The app automatically **drops the trailing interval** if it is narrower
  than your chosen interval width, or if it reaches the current calendar
  year — records published in a year still in progress are necessarily
  undercounted (the year has not finished), and an artificially low $S_i$ in
  the most recent interval would otherwise bias the fitted trend. This
  matches the convention used in the source manuscript's own scripts.

# Using the App — Step by Step

## Login

Enter the shared password on the landing page. There are no individual user
accounts; anyone with the password has full access.

## Tab 1 — Data & Setup

1. Choose **Group type**: Parasitic or Free-living. This determines which
   data columns are required and which model structures are available later.
2. Enter a **Taxon name** — free text, used only to label plots and the
   downloadable report.
3. **Upload** your `.xlsx`/`.csv` file. A validation banner confirms the row
   count or reports the first missing/invalid column.
4. If your file has recognizable taxonomic-hierarchy or habitat columns, an
   optional **Category** and/or **Habitat** dropdown appears — e.g. pick
   rank `family` = `Dactylogyridae`, and/or habitat = `agua doce` (freshwater);
   a status box reports the effect, along with any automatic
   `taxonomicStatus`/`taxonRank` filtering (§3.3).
5. Set the **interval width** (in years) that species counts are aggregated
   into (e.g., 3 or 5 years — matching the interval width used in the
   Dactylogyridae/Actinopterygii analyses). Smaller intervals give more data
   points but noisier per-interval counts; larger intervals smooth noise but
   reduce the number of time points available to fit the trend.
6. Optionally set a **start year** / **end year** to restrict the modeled
   window (defaults to the full range present in your data).
7. In parasitic mode, enter **$H_t$** — your best estimate of the total host
   species pool, as a plain number (not fitted). Only required if you plan
   to fit a host structure.
8. Review the **aggregated interval table** at the bottom of the page — this
   is the exact $S_i$/$T_i$/$\text{cumS}_i$(/$\text{cumH}_i$) time series that
   will be passed to the model. Check it for implausible jumps or gaps before
   proceeding. Below it, two data-only diagnostic plots (no model fit
   required) update live as you change the settings above: **effort vs.
   discovery** (does more taxonomist effort track more species described?)
   and **effort trend over time** (is taxonomist effort itself rising,
   falling, or flat across your study period?) — see §5 for how to read
   both.

## Tab 2 — Priors & Run

1. **Structures to fit**: up to six checkboxes (parasitic mode) or four
   (free-living mode) — see §2.3, including the two optional
   Negative-Binomial structures. The app pre-selects more than one so a
   comparison (§2.5) is produced by default; uncheck down to a single
   structure if you only want one model's diagnostics.
2. **Single run vs. battery**: leave "Run full sensitivity battery" unchecked
   for a fast run with one prior specification (recommended for initial
   exploration). Check it to instead define and compare several full prior
   scenarios (step 5 below).
3. **Single-run priors**: enter the Gamma($\alpha$, $\beta$) prior for $S_T$
   (no default — see §2.2 and the guidance box below) and the $\beta$
   (trend) prior, shared by both trend forms. Two more prior blocks appear
   *only* for the trend form(s) your selected structures actually need:
   log($L_0$) (exponential trend) and/or $L_0$ (linear trend, natural scale
   — typically a very small number; see the numerical-stability note in
   §2.3 for scaling guidance). The Negative-Binomial dispersion parameter
   $\phi$ has no prior field here — it is always fit with a fixed prior
   (§2.3).

   > **Choosing $\alpha$/$\beta$ for the $S_T$ prior:** the Gamma
   > distribution's mean is $\alpha/\beta$. A simple approach: pick a rough
   > expected total species count $m$ from external knowledge (a comparable
   > taxon, an expert guess, a published order-of-magnitude estimate), pick a
   > shape $\alpha$ reflecting your confidence (larger $\alpha$ = tighter,
   > more confident prior; $\alpha \approx 20$–100 is a reasonably informative
   > but not overly rigid choice), then set $\beta = \alpha / m$. The prior's
   > lower bound is automatically constrained to exceed your observed
   > cumulative species count, so $S_T$ can never be estimated below what
   > you've already described.

4. **Negative-Binomial $S_T$ prior mode** (only shown when a
   Negative-Binomial structure is selected, single-run mode only): leave
   "Use a bounded (flat) prior instead of Gamma" unchecked to use the same
   Gamma prior as above for $S_T$, or check it to switch to the bounded/flat
   mode instead (§2.3) — optionally overriding the lower/upper bounds
   (blank = observed total + 10 / observed total $\times$ 10). Only affects
   the Negative-Binomial structure(s) you've selected; any Poisson structure
   in the same run always uses the Gamma prior above.
5. **Battery scenarios**: fill in the scenario form (name, shared $S_T$/
   $\beta$ priors, plus both the exponential-trend and linear-trend
   efficiency priors — whichever your selected structures need for that
   scenario gets used) and click "Add scenario"; repeat for each scenario
   you want compared. In parasitic mode, each scenario also has an optional
   **Ht override**: leave it blank to use the Tab 1 $H_t$ for that scenario,
   or set a different value to test how sensitive your $S_T$ estimate is to
   the host-pool assumption (§2.3's practical note) — e.g. one scenario at
   the documented $H_t$ and another at a higher estimated $H_t$, each with
   its own matching $S_T$ prior, replicating the source manuscript's
   Conservative-vs-Extrapolated comparison in a single run. "Clear all
   scenarios" resets the list. Battery scenarios always use the Gamma prior
   for $S_T$, including for any Negative-Binomial structure selected.
6. **MCMC settings**: default iterations (4000) and warmup (2000) with 4
   chains are adequate for exploration; check "Full precision" (20000/10000)
   for a final, publication-quality run once you're satisfied with your setup
   — this is substantially slower.
7. Click **Run analysis**. Only one analysis runs at a time across *all*
   users of the app (a shared compute worker) — if others are running jobs,
   yours will start once theirs finishes. The status box shows elapsed time
   while waiting/running.

## Tab 3 — Results

Whichever structures you fit, each shows:

- **Parameter table**: mean, 95% credible interval, and convergence
  diagnostics (`Rhat`, `n_eff`) for $S_T$, the efficiency parameter(s), and
  $\beta$.
- **Posterior histogram** and **trace plot** for $S_T$ — the trace plot
  should look like a "hairy caterpillar" with no trend or stuck chains; if
  it doesn't, increase iterations/warmup.
- **Simulated vs. observed plot** (posterior predictive check): blue lines
  are simulated discovery-rate trajectories drawn from the fitted model; the
  red line is your actual observed data. The red line should sit
  comfortably within the cloud of blue lines if the model fits well.
- **Species vs. effort, simulated vs. observed**: the same posterior-
  predictive draws (Si_rep) plotted against each interval's *observed*
  effort ($T_i$) instead of time — blue cloud = simulated species counts
  at each interval's effort level, red points/line = your actual observed
  (T_i, S_i) pairs. This is the effort-axis counterpart of the
  simulated-vs-observed plot above.
- **Percent-described plot**: the posterior distribution of
  (observed total) / $S_T$, i.e., what fraction of the estimated true
  diversity has been described so far.
- **Extrapolation plot**: your observed cumulative-discovery curve, plus a
  forward projection (with 95% credible band) assuming future taxonomic
  effort continues at the recent average level.

If **two or more structures** were fit — the default for a single run, and
always for a battery — a **Structure comparison** section appears first,
with a ranked table (LOO-ELPD, CRPS, MAE, $H_t$, $S_T$ estimate per
structure/scenario — $H_t$ is blank for no-host structures, and shows
exactly which host-pool assumption produced each row's $S_T$), the
ELPD-difference and CRPS/MAE comparison plots, and the LOO-ELPD-vs-CRPS
rank-concordance plot (§2.5), with the best-supported structure called out
explicitly.

## Tab 4 — Download Report

Generates a single self-contained HTML file bundling every figure, the
parameter table(s), the methods description, and a data-handling notice —
built fresh from your current results, never stored server-side. Useful for
supplementary material, sharing with collaborators, or your own records.

## Manual / About

The Manual tab offers this document as a downloadable, print-quality PDF
(math and Greek letters render as real typeset LaTeX, not browser-dependent
web fonts). About is a short in-app summary of scope and data handling.

# Interpreting the Diagnostic Plots (Reference)

| Plot | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Posterior histogram ($S_T$) | A unimodal, reasonably concentrated distribution. A histogram that looks identical to your prior means the data contributed little information — consider a longer/less sparse time series or a more informative prior. |
| Trace plot | Overlapping, stationary "hairy caterpillar" traces across chains, no drift or sudden jumps. |
| Simulated vs. observed | Red observed line inside the blue simulation envelope, most of the time. Persistent misses indicate model misspecification (e.g., wrong host/trend-form choice, or an interval width that's too coarse/fine). |
| Percent-described | Sanity-check this against domain knowledge — an implausibly low or high percentage may indicate a prior that's too far from the data (revisit $\alpha$/$\beta$). |
| Extrapolation | The credible band should widen (not narrow) further into the future — a band that stays razor-thin suggests overconfidence, usually from an overly tight $S_T$ prior. |
| Effort vs. discovery scatter (Tab 1, data-only) | A rough positive relationship supports the model's core assumption that more taxonomists means more species found. A flat or negative relationship is a warning sign worth investigating before trusting $S_T$. |
| Effort trend (Tab 1, data-only) | Whether raw taxonomist effort ($T_i$) is itself rising, falling, or flat over time — check this before over-interpreting the fitted efficiency trend ($\beta$), since a trend in effort and a trend in per-taxonomist efficiency can otherwise be conflated. |
| Species vs. effort, simulated vs. observed (Tab 3, per fitted structure) | Same idea as "Simulated vs. observed" above but on the effort axis: the red observed points/trend should sit inside the blue simulated cloud. A model that fits the time series (first plot) but not this one suggests the effort covariate itself is poorly captured by the fitted structure. |
| LOO-ELPD / CRPS / MAE (structure comparison) | Prefer structures that rank well on **both** ELPD and CRPS; large disagreement between the two metrics for a given structure is itself informative (see §2.5 and the source manuscript's discussion of this exact situation). |
| Rank-concordance plot (structure comparison, 2+ models) | Close agreement (small vertical gaps) between the CRPS-rank and ELPD-rank lines, especially near rank 1, means the two scoring rules agree on the best model. Wide gaps for a specific model mean the two metrics disagree on it — don't lean on that model's ranking from a single metric alone. |

# Data Handling & Privacy

- **Nothing is stored.** Your uploaded file, the fitted model object, and
  every generated figure exist only in your browser session's server-side
  scratch space, in memory/temp-disk for the lifetime of that session.
- **No database.** The application does not use any persistent database —
  not for your data, not for results, not even temporarily.
- **Session end = deletion.** When your browser tab closes or the session
  times out, all session data is deleted automatically.
- **You must download before leaving.** The report (Tab 4) is the only way
  to keep a copy of your results; nothing is retrievable after the session
  ends.
- **Authentication** uses a single shared password (not stored in plaintext
  anywhere in the deployed application — only its SHA-256 hash is kept as a
  server secret) and a per-session flag; there are no individual accounts,
  audit logs, or password-reset flows.

# Troubleshooting / FAQ

**"Missing required column(s)" on upload.**
Column names must match exactly, including case (`scientificName`, not
`ScientificName` or `Scientific_Name`). Check §3 for the exact required set
per mode.

**Category dropdown doesn't appear.**
It only appears when your file contains at least one recognized taxonomic
rank column (§3.3: `phylum` through `subGenus`). If your file is already a
minimal, pre-filtered species list, this is expected — no action needed.

**"No usable rows" after selecting a Category.**
Check the category value spelling/case matches your data exactly (the
dropdown is populated from your file's own values, so this should be rare),
and remember taxonomicStatus/taxonRank filters (if those columns exist,
matched against either CTFB or Darwin Core vocabulary — see §3.3) apply on
top of your category choice.

**"Fewer than 3 usable time intervals after aggregation."**
Your data, after filtering and interval aggregation, doesn't span enough
distinct time buckets to fit a trend. Widen your start/end year range, or
reduce the interval width.

**Run seems stuck on "Running…".**
Only one analysis runs at a time across all users — you may be queued behind
another user's job, especially a full-precision or battery run. There is no
separate progress bar for queue position; the elapsed-time counter includes
any wait.

**High `Rhat` / low `n_eff` warnings.**
Increase iterations and warmup (or enable "Full precision"), and/or
double-check that your priors aren't so tight that they conflict sharply
with the data (this can create hard-to-sample posterior geometry). The
*host + linear* structure is particularly prone to this — see the
numerical-stability note in §2.3 — as is any Negative-Binomial structure
run in bounded (flat) $S_T$-prior mode (§2.3's Negative-Binomial note).

**"Enter a valid $S_T$/log($L_0$)/$L_0$ prior" error on Run.**
The app deliberately has no default $S_T$ prior (§2.2), and only validates
the efficiency-intercept prior(s) your *currently selected* structures
actually need — fill in whichever block(s) are showing.

**Host structures unavailable in my mode.**
Host structures require a supplied `Ht` value and are only available in
Parasitic mode; Free-living mode always uses no-host structures only.

# Glossary

- **$S_T$** — total number of species estimated to exist in the group (the
  primary output of the model).
- **Structure** — one of up to six model variants: host term on/off crossed
  with exponential/linear efficiency-trend form, plus an optional
  Negative-Binomial likelihood for the no-host forms (§2.3).
- **$H_t$** — total known/expected host-species pool (host structures only);
  a fixed number you supply, not fitted. Overridable per battery scenario
  (§4.3) to sensitivity-test how much $S_T$ depends on this assumption.
- **Category filter** — optional restriction of a full taxonomic export to
  one rank/value (e.g. family = "Dactylogyridae") before analysis (§3.3).
- **Habitat filter** — optional restriction to one habitat/environment
  value (e.g. `habitat` = "agua doce", freshwater) before analysis (§3.3).
- **Interval** — a fixed-width block of consecutive years (e.g., a 5-year
  bin) used to aggregate species counts for model fitting.
- **Effort ($T_i$)** — number of unique describing taxonomists active in an
  interval, used as a proxy for research intensity.
- **Credible interval (CrI)** — the Bayesian analogue of a confidence
  interval; a 95% CrI means the posterior probability that the true value
  lies in that range is 95%, given the model and data.
- **LOO-ELPD** — Leave-One-Out Expected Log Predictive Density; a Bayesian
  model-comparison metric estimating out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
- **CRPS / MAE** — Continuous Ranked Probability Score / Mean Absolute Error;
  metrics comparing a model's simulated predictions to observed data.
- **Rhat, n_eff** — MCMC convergence diagnostics; see §2.4.
- **$\phi$ (phi)** — Negative Binomial dispersion parameter (Negative-Binomial
  structures only); larger values are closer to Poisson. Fit with a fixed
  prior, not user-configurable (§2.3).
